entries.market_reading: A comparative claim about how much cash the business produces. With no comparator stated, the market reads 'cash flow' as operating cash flow, usually alongside free cash flow, and reads 'low' as low against the company's own recent level, against its earnings or revenue, against its peers, or against what it has to pay out. A dollar figure alone is never low or high: for a company of Apple's size the absolute amount is large on any scale, so 'is Apple's cash flow low' can only be answered by naming the comparison.

entries.formula: Resolve to operating cash flow (CF-02) and free cash flow = operating cash flow - capital expenditure (CF-03). Then express each against the comparators in frame_notes: the change against prior periods, the ratio to net income (CF-08), the ratio to revenue (CF-06), and coverage of dividends and buybacks (CF-25, CF-26).
entries.period_convention: Trailing twelve months (TTM) or the latest fiscal year. TTM from one 10-Q plus the last 10-K: prior fiscal year + current YTD - prior-year comparable YTD (the 10-Q carries the comparable YTD, S-X 10-01(c)(3)). Trend: year-over-year on the same basis; history: 3-5 fiscal years (a 10-K carries three years of cash flows, two for smaller reporting companies).
entries.frame_notes: history: below the company's own level. Compare the TTM or latest fiscal year with the prior year and with its 3-5 year average; the SEC's MD&A guidance speaks of the indicative value of historical cash flows. scale: cash per dollar of revenue (OCF or FCF margin) or per dollar of net income (conversion). This is what makes companies of different sizes comparable. peers: a margin or conversion below the median of same-industry filers, on the same TTM basis. obligations: FCF short of dividends plus buybacks, of committed capex, or of debt due within 12 months (S-K 303(b)(1)(ii)). absolute: only the sign stands alone. Negative operating cash flow means operations consumed cash, and MD&A must identify that condition.
entries.direction: higher is better for the same business; a fall is read against its cause (working-capital timing, a one-off payment, or higher capex, which lowers FCF but not OCF)

entries.notes: Routing rule for Case. A bare 'cash flow' question answers with OCF and FCF side by side, each with its comparator named. 'Low' or 'high' with no comparator defaults to two frames that need no peer set and no price: history (the company's own trend) and scale (margin and conversion). Peers need a defined peer group. Market-value frames need a price the desk can cite (CF-07). Observed in the tree: vocabulary 0.4 maps the neutral term 'operating cash flow' to the directional proposition 'operations consume cash' (operating_cash_burn), and 'cashflow' written as one word is not among its terms. So 'is apple cashflow low' matches nothing, and 'what is apple's operating cash flow' would be read as a burn claim.

entries.formula: Operating cash flow - capital expenditure (purchases of PP&E), both for the same duration. Label every variant: less capitalized software or intangibles; plus proceeds from asset sales ('net capex'); less acquisitions; less finance-lease principal.

Asset lines (receivables, inventories, operating capital; balance credit) are positive when the asset grew, which USED cash; liability lines (payables, accrued liabilities, contract liabilities; balance debit) are positive when the liability grew, which PROVIDED cash. The face of the statement shows asset increases as negative numbers.

entries.market_reading: How many months the company can keep operating at its current burn before its cash runs out: cash (often plus short-term investments) divided by monthly net burn. Case shows runway months on N1 (cash and equivalents) and N2 (N1 plus current short-term investments), names the one used, and states the burn basis (operating cash flow, or operating cash flow less capex), the window (latest quarter or TTM) and the balance-sheet date. Case sets that figure against the 12-month horizons as comparisons, each labelled with its owner: S-K Item 303(b)(1)'s short-term disclosure horizon (the SEC's), measured from the most recent fiscal period end; ASC 205-40's one-year going-concern window from issuance (FASB's, by reference); and AS 2415's auditor window (PCAOB's). None of these is a sufficiency line. Case draws no 'enough cash' line and gives no 'will need to raise' or 'running out' verdict. The company's own MD&A statement of whether its cash suffices for the next 12 months is the primary evidence, cited as management's.

Case always shows both numerators at the same date and names the one used: N1 = cash and cash equivalents (CashAndCashEquivalentsAtCarryingValue); N2 = N1 + ShortTermInvestments, else MarketableSecuritiesCurrent. Undrawn committed credit is shown beside it, never added. State the burn basis (operating cash flow, or operating cash flow less capex) and the window. entries.period_convention: Cash at the latest balance-sheet date; burn from the latest discrete quarter or TTM. The cash date must not be older than the end of the burn period (the Case v0.4 rule).
entries.frame_notes: obligations: runway against debt maturities and committed spending; the 12-month horizons (S-K 303(b)(1), the SEC's, from the most recent fiscal period end; ASC 205-40, FASB's, from issuance; AS 2415, PCAOB's, from the audited statements' date) are shown beside it as comparisons, each labelled with its owner, never as a sufficiency line. history: runway shortening across quarters.
entries.direction: higher (longer) is better

thresholds.line: the next 12 months from the most recent fiscal period end: the SEC's MD&A short-term disclosure horizon (S-K 303(b)(1)); a comparison horizon, not a runway sufficiency line
thresholds.meaning: The horizon over which management must analyse its ability to obtain adequate cash (S-K Item 303(b)(1)). The SEC draws no sufficiency line and no runway line. Case shows runway months against it as a comparison, labelled as the SEC's, with no pass or fail. If Case v0.4's 12-month line is kept, it is labelled as Siglia's own display line, never as the SEC's

thresholds.line: one year after the financial statements are issued
thresholds.meaning: The going-concern evaluation window management applies (FASB ASC 205-40, by reference). It is one of three twelve-month clocks: S-K 303(b)(1) runs from the most recent fiscal period end (S4); ASC 205-40 from the date the statements are issued; PCAOB AS 2415 .02 from the date of the audited statements ('not to exceed one year beyond the date of the financial statements being audited', S69). Case reports the filed conclusion and does not make it: management's substantial-doubt disclosure, including whether management's plans alleviate the doubt (SubstantialDoubtAboutGoingConcernWithinOneYear where the filer tags it, otherwise the note text; an absent tag reads 'cannot establish', never 'no doubt'), and the auditor's explanatory paragraph. Substantial doubt weighs conditions and events in the aggregate against management's plans, and negative operating cash flow is one example condition among several (AS 2415 .06). So a runway under 12 months is not a going-concern finding, a going-concern disclosure is not the filed form of a short runway, and this window is never used as a runway cutoff

CFI's start-up guidance (a training provider): 6-12 months is a common runway aim for private companies, and some VCs advise more than 18. Labelled as CFI's; not authoritative and not a line for a public company

notes: How to read this family. (1) 'Cash flow is low' is always a comparative claim. There is no authoritative level below which a positive cash flow is 'low'; only the sign of operating cash flow is definitional. Case should answer with the comparator named. By default use history (the company's own trend) and scale (margin, conversion), which need neither a peer set nor a price. (2) Plain 'free cash flow' means operating cash flow minus purchases of PP&E. It is after interest and taxes paid, both of which are inside US GAAP operating cash flow. 'Unlevered' or 'to the firm' means FCFF; 'to equity' means FCFE. 'Levered' is ambiguous: most definitions add net borrowing, while some screens mean plain OCF minus capex. State which. (3) THE 10-Q YEAR-TO-DATE TRAP (S-X 10-01(c)(3); 8-03 for smaller reporting companies). Interim cash-flow statements cover the fiscal year to date, not the quarter, while income statements give both. Discrete quarters must be differenced from YTD values (Q4 = FY - 9M). A TTM can be built from one 10-Q and the last 10-K: FY + current YTD - prior-year comparable YTD. Use the fact's context dates, never the form type. A condensed 10-Q may also fold small lines such as capex into others (S-X 10-01(a)(4)). A proposed semiannual Form 10-S (91 FR 24968, not adopted) would add six-month-only filers. (4) SIGNS. Payments* and Proceeds* elements are filed as positive magnitudes and the direction is in the name. NetCashProvidedByUsedIn* is signed as filed. IncreaseDecreaseIn* elements carry the change in the BALANCE: asset lines have balance credit, so positive means the asset grew and cash was used; liability lines have balance debit, so positive means cash was provided. The face of the statement shows the opposite sign for asset lines. (5) TAXONOMY DRIFT. SalesRevenueNet, CostOfGoodsSold, the ExcessTaxBenefitFromShareBasedCompensation* lines and CashAndCashEquivalentsPeriodIncreaseDecrease are in the 2016 taxonomy and absent from 2026 (verified on FASB's schema files). History queries need the old names. (6) Company-reported FCF is a non-GAAP liquidity measure (Reg G; S-K 10(e)). In filings it must be reconciled to OCF, cannot exclude cash-settled charges, and cannot be per share. The desk computes its own from the GAAP lines and labels any company figure 'company-defined'. (7) LICENCES. CFR, Federal Register and US Code text is PD and quoted within 25 words. FASB taxonomy element names are used as identifiers only (OD). ASC and ASU, CFA, S&P, the academic papers, CFI, Wall Street Prep, Damodaran, BDC and Berkshire are by reference only, with formulas written in Siglia's words and no text stored. (8) no_market_threshold semantics used here: true when no Tier 1 source draws a line for the concept. Practitioner rules of thumb (OCF/NI >= 1.0x; DSO < 45 days; capex/depreciation near 100%; 6-12 months of runway) are recorded as kind 'rule-of-thumb' and never presented as authoritative. (9) Frames vocabulary: history = the company against its own past; scale = against its own revenue, earnings, assets or market value; peers = against same-industry filers on the same period basis; obligations = against what it must pay (dividends, buybacks, capex commitments, debt, burn); absolute = the sign or a source-drawn line. (10) Observed in the tree while researching (not sources). The cash_conversion derivation has no guard for net income <= 0. (11) Practitioner formula errors to avoid copying: WSP's cash conversion ratio page writes the formula as net income / CFO while its example and rule use CFO / net income. CFI and WSP write net burn as receipts minus spending, the reverse of the burn sign.
